title: The rooster crows (Luke 22:54–62)
hook: Peter swears three times he never knew him, then the rooster, then the look

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gethsemane: take this cup, and then, not my will. Your line was not my will. Where did you loosen your grip? That same night, soldiers come to the garden. Day sixty-seven.

Pretending not to know someone. Laughing along. Keeping quiet when you meant to speak. It can happen in a second, before anyone has decided anything. A courtyard in Jerusalem, in the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house. Mark says the others fled. But Peter, Peter who walked on water, Peter who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, follows at a distance. He slips into the courtyard and sits down by a fire with the servants and guards, warming his hands. Today, the rooster crows.
screen: `PRETENDING NOT TO KNOW SOMEONE.` → `ARRESTED IN THE NIGHT.` → `PETER BY THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: A servant girl looks at him in the firelight and says: this man was with him. And Peter, in the King James Bible: "Woman, I know him not." A little later someone else: you're one of them. "Man, I am not." About an hour later, a third person insists: surely this fellow was with him, for he's a Galilean. And Peter says: "Man, I know not what thou sayest." And while he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Earlier that evening Jesus had told him exactly this, and Peter had said never. Then Luke adds a detail no other Gospel has: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." Across the courtyard, their eyes meet. Luke doesn't describe the look. Angry? Sad? Loving? The sources are silent. "And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." And this story is in all four Gospels. The first Christians could have left out the night Peter failed. Instead all four kept it. Peter, the rock, the one with the keys, is also the one who said three times, I don't know him. Failure isn't where Peter's story ends. Tradition links the rooster on top of some church steeples to this night: a reminder to stay awake, and that even Peter fell, and was not finished.
screen: `WOMAN, I KNOW HIM NOT.` · `THREE TIMES, THEN THE ROOSTER.` · `THE LORD TURNED AND LOOKED.` · `TOLD IN ALL FOUR GOSPELS.` · then, large: `PETER WENT OUT, AND WEPT BITTERLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one old failure you still carry. A time you let someone down, or yourself. Not to replay it. Just to look at it once, honestly. Now notice how long you've been carrying it. Think of Peter weeping in the dark, and remember that his story didn't end there. Try saying to yourself, quietly: that happened, and I'm more than that. If you pray, you can ask to be forgiven and to forgive yourself. The bell holds the time.
The rooster crows. Three denials by a fire, a rooster, a look across the courtyard, and a man weeping bitterly, who wasn't finished.
Your line: even peter. Today, when you remember the old failure, let it be a story that goes on, not one that ends there. Day sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Peter's denial is read in Holy Week in many churches, and it's sung in the Passion settings of Bach and others. Weathervanes shaped like roosters sit on some church steeples, especially in Europe.

myth: only one Gospel tells of Peter's denial
all four tell it. the early church didn't hide it.

Luke says he turned and looked, and never says how. the sources are silent.

the third accuser said he was a Galilean. Matthew adds that his speech gave him away.

fork.setup: you're Peter, by the fire. twice you've said you don't know him. now a third person insists: surely you were with him, you're a Galilean. what do you say?

get up and walk away without a word.
fork.reveal: he denies it a third time, and the rooster crows. the Lord turns and looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.

original.note: Greek: a rooster. The bird that crowed after Peter's third denial.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter's big failure.
what it means: Peter denies him three times, meets his eyes, and weeps, and the story doesn't end there.
what a scholar hears: all four Gospels keep this embarrassing story about Peter, and only Luke has the look across the courtyard.

notes: 'In all four Gospels' (Matthew 26:69–75; Mark 14:66–72; Luke 22:54–62; John 18:15–27). The look (22:61) is unique to Luke.
The rooster on church steeples as a symbol linked to Peter; commonly stated (a ninth-century papal decree is often cited). Confirm.
Bach's St Matthew and St John Passions include the denial ('Erbarme dich' follows it in the St Matthew). Confirm howItsDone.
The practice invites self-forgiveness and does not tell the listener what to believe; 'if you pray' framing.
Carry is lowercase 'even peter' in the index; kept exactly.

Fresh review (days 57–74): fixed an attribution error, the Galilean accent ('thy speech bewrayeth thee') is Matthew 26:73, not Luke, so the teach now follows Luke 22:59 and only the myth reveal mentions Matthew. Hook drops 'Think of' and 'Most of us'; cut 'its most famous leader', 'told it everywhere', 'courage for two thousand years' and 'many church steeples'; the rooster-steeple link is given as tradition.
